If you didn't read the previous story, basically I wrecked a 32 ton vehicle because my vehicle commander told me shut the fuck up and floor it, and I wasn't able to warn him of the ditch we were cruising for at 40-50 MPH. He had to get 6 stitches in his knee.

On this particular day, I was the CQ runner, and our company ran an imbiss - a snack bar, with profits going to the FRG. It was COB, and I was counting the imbiss money before we closed up shop, when someone came over and snatched the money out of my hand. I was sitting in a chair, and I cooked back to punch whoever just snatched the money, but I looked up and it was the company Mike Golf. So I'm sitting here, fist ready to strike. It was after COB, so NCOs and officers liked to hang out after we were released because everyone hates them, including their families, and they didn't like shedding their uniforms, and my squad leader was standing right there.

"PFC Peen, you better not let that E7 take your money, you better do something about that!"

All the company leadership is standing around, just waiting to see what happens. I look that Mike Golf in the face, and he gives me this slow head shake of "you better not do something", and I fucking punch that mother fucker right on the side of the face.

His head jerks back, and he comes right back with a fist right into my face. I was sitting in a swivel chair, so I'm pretty sure I spun around. He had this look of "Oh shit, what did I do???" on his face, dropped the money, and he ran into his office and shut the door. Reminder: he could have lost his career for the time he threw a sledge hammer at me, and he just punched that same person in the face. I mean, it was justified, I hit him first, but he panicked as soon as he punched me back.

Everyone is laughing, including me. I go to the bathroom to wash the blood off my face, and noticed that my lip is split, like bad. My lower lip was no longer connected to itself.

I go back to the CQ desk and tell the NCO that I need to go to the aid station for stitches. I didn't realize this at the time, but my company commander was standing there the whole time and watched the whole thing go down. I mean, I realized it, but I didn't process it, I saw him there the whole time.

"Peen," he says with a jolly ol' smile, "what happened, why do you need stitches?"

Well obviously I punched your Mike Golf, and he punched back harder, "Sir, I walked into a door."

"Good shit!"

I walked to the aid station and told them the same story.

"No you didn't walk into a door, tell me what happened."

I told him again, the God honest truth. I'm just clumsy, and walked into a door.

"Fucking infantry."

I don't know what to make of that story. I got to punch an asshole E7 in the face or that some asshole private got 3 stitches in return for the 6 stitches he gave an NCO. Either way, the part I found the funniest was how the CO handled it. I fucking loved that dude.

He ordered me to attack the XO once, and I had been roughed up enough at that point in my career as a private, so I said, "Sir, I don't believe that is a legal order." He confirmed, but then firmly said, "When we are on the battlefield, I expect you to follow all of my orders, whether or not you believe they are legal or not."

I would have too. He was a great fucking leader. He knew the names of every soldier under him, and even though I rarely talked to him, he knew how things were going with my girlfriend or if I had broken up. He basically made the lives of everyone he was in command of his business.

....aaaaand one week into Iraq and he's dead. His replacement was a piece of shit that I contemplated killing on multiple occasions.

Not one of my usual stories with a beginning or an end, but just something about sleep.

In the infantry, I learned how to sleep whenever and wherever. I would fall asleep when I didn't even want to.

I remember one time in Iraq, we rolled in from mission, I was driving the Bradley, and as soon as I killed the engine, I was out. My NCO said he looked through the hell hole, and was like, "no fucking way he's sleeping in that position." My face was smashed onto the front driver's periscope. That fucker left me there, said that I looked comfortable and he didn't want to wake me.

We were ran ragged that deployment. 48 hour mission, come back, refit, and just wait for the call, usually a few hours later. Our platoon was split into two patrol groups, but we were short handed, so a few of us were on both patrol groups and on every single mission.

One night we roll in, and in my head I did the calculations - go upstairs, 2 mins; gear down, 30 secs; get called up on mission and gear up, 3-4 mins; get down to the vehicles, 2 mins - anyway, it was far too much time I was willing to sacrifice, so I just passed the fuck out in position in the HMMWV. My platoon sergeant was leaving the showers, walking by and woke me up, "Ready to roll, sergeant!"

"What the fuck are you doing?"

"Well, I figured it would take me 10 minutes to gear down, and 10 minutes to gear back up, that's 20 minutes of sleep I'd be missing out on, so I just slept here."

He shook his head like we were nuts. That's when I became aware that I wasn't the only one who fell asleep in the vehicle. I attempted to fall back asleep, but then our platoon sergeant came back out a few minutes later in full kit saying that we had to roll back out. A smile of "I told you so" rolled over me, and then despair.

I could find a rock in the field, call it a pillow, and be out in seconds...

It was never on deployments or field problems that I had a problem sleeping, it was always in garrison, or now that I've been out.

I don't know what it is, but I can never sleep. I don't understand it. I remember on actual missions, like where we could die, "hey, I'm going to pass out for a few minutes, wake me up if something happens, and we'll trade off.", but then, when I have the opportunity to get uninterrupted sleep, I just can't.

I kind of know. In the field there was always a bro on watch. In garrison, and now civilian life, no one is on watch.

I miss sleeping on edge, where I was always seconds away from being told to gear up. It made sleep a priority, and I could force sleep upon myself.
